claims.text: High configurational entropy kinetically stabilizes a metastable single-phase random solid solution at elevated temperatures.
Inherent lattice distortions kinetically stabilize the metastable random solid solution at elevated temperatures.
Entropy- and distortion-based stabilization delays atomic segregation.
Entropy- and distortion-based stabilization delays oxidation.
Above a critical temperature, local enthalpic interactions promote short-range ordering.
Above a critical temperature, local enthalpic interactions promote phase separation.
The initial nanoparticles are a single-phase random FCC solid solution.
The initial nanoparticles have an equiatomic or near-equiatomic elemental distribution.
The initial nanoparticles have a narrow particle-size distribution of approximately 10–20 nm.
Local lattice distortions impede atomic diffusion.
The random distribution of multiple elements impedes the formation of phase boundaries.
At moderate high temperatures, high configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion hinder elemental aggregation.
At moderate high temperatures, high configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion hinder oxidation.
At a critical temperature, favorable interactions between particular elemental pairs overcome entropic stabilization.
The critical temperature is anticipated to be approximately 400–500 °C.
Below the critical temperature, the nanoalloy will retain a random solid solution with minimal ordering.
Below the critical temperature, the nanoalloy will exhibit minimal oxidation.
Above the critical temperature, new diffraction peaks attributable to ordering or phase separation will appear.
Above the critical temperature, chemical-state signatures will indicate degraded chemical stability relative to the lower-temperature state.
The proposed behavior is bounded to high-entropy nanoalloys with particle sizes of 10–20 nm under controlled oxygen-free conditions.

contradictions.description: The experiment is explicitly oxygen-free, yet oxidation and oxidation-state changes are used as central measures of chemical degradation. Without an identified oxygen source or pre-existing oxide, the proposed inert-atmosphere treatment cannot cleanly test resistance to oxidation.
